objectives: Describe energy stores, transfers and how energy is wasted.
Calculate kinetic, gravitational potential and elastic potential energy.
Use the specific heat capacity, power and efficiency equations.

questions.a: Energy spread out to the surroundings (usually by heating), so it is less useful.

engage.title: LEARNING OBJECTIVES
engage.hook: Today: four big ideas from P1 Energy, then you show what you know.
engage.content:
1. Describe how energy moves between stores, and why some is wasted.
2. Calculate kinetic, gravitational potential and elastic potential energy.
3. Calculate the energy needed to heat something (specific heat capacity).
4. Calculate power and efficiency.

items: kinetic (moving) · gravitational potential (raised up) · elastic potential (stretched)
thermal (hot) · chemical (food, fuel, batteries) · nuclear · magnetic · electrostatic
mechanically (a force) · electrically (a current) · by heating · by radiation (light, sound)
Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred.
Wasted energy is dissipated to the surroundings, usually by heating.
Reduce waste: lubrication (less friction), thermal insulation (thicker walls, low thermal conductivity).

check.q: Which energy store increases when a ball is lifted up?
State the law of conservation of energy.
check.a: Energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred from one store to another.

check.q: Give one way to reduce unwanted energy transfer in a machine.

items: m = mass (kg), g = 9.8 N/kg, h = height (m)

check.q: A 2 kg ball moves at 3 m/s. Calculate its kinetic energy.
A 5 kg box is lifted 2 m. g = 9.8 N/kg. Calculate the GPE gained.
A spring (k = 40 N/m) is stretched by 0.1 m. Calculate the elastic potential energy.

learn.heading: Specific heat capacity
learn.example: Specific heat capacity is the energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C. Heating 2 kg of water (c = 4200 J/kg °C) by 10 °C needs 2 \times 4200 \times 10 = 84 000 J.

check.q: What does specific heat capacity mean?
check.a: The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 °C.

check.q: 1 kg of oil (c = 2000 J/kg °C) warms by 5 °C. Calculate the energy transferred.
Same energy, same mass: which warms up more, a substance with a high or a low specific heat capacity?
check.a: The one with the LOW specific heat capacity.

items: Power is how fast energy is transferred.
P = {E/t}  (energy in J, time in s)
Never more than 1 (100%): some energy is always wasted.

check.q: What is the unit of power?
A motor transfers 1200 J in 60 s. Calculate its power.
A lamp takes in 50 J and gives out 10 J as light. Calculate its efficiency.

developing.q: A skateboarder of mass 50 kg rolls down a ramp 2.0 m high. g = 9.8 N/kg. Calculate the gravitational potential energy she loses.
Describe the energy transfers as the skateboarder rolls down the ramp and then slows to a stop at the bottom.
developing.a: Her gravitational potential energy store decreases and her kinetic energy store increases. As she slows down, friction and air resistance transfer energy to the thermal store of the surroundings (it is dissipated).
starters: As she rolls down, her ... store decreases and ...

developing.q: 0.2 kg of water is heated from 20 °C to 70 °C. c = 4200 J/kg °C. Calculate the energy transferred to the water.
A hairdryer has a power of 1500 W. Calculate the energy it transfers in 120 s.
A motor takes in 400 J of energy. 300 J is useful. Calculate its efficiency.

reaching.q: A 0.06 kg ball is thrown upwards at 12 m/s. (a) Calculate its kinetic energy. (b) Assume no energy is wasted. Calculate the maximum height it reaches. g = 9.8 N/kg.
A spring with spring constant 200 N/m is stretched by 15 cm. Calculate the elastic potential energy stored.
A 2000 W heater warms a 1.5 kg aluminium block for 60 s. c = 900 J/kg °C. Assume all the energy heats the block. Calculate the temperature rise.
Give two advantages and two disadvantages of generating electricity with solar panels.
reaching.a: Advantages (any two): renewable; no carbon dioxide released while running; low running costs. Disadvantages (any two): no electricity at night and less when cloudy (unreliable); needs a large area; high cost to set up.

mastering.q: A 600 kg rollercoaster car starts at rest at the top of a 20 m drop. At the bottom its speed is 18 m/s. g = 9.8 N/kg. (a) Calculate the GPE lost. (b) Calculate the kinetic energy at the bottom. (c) Calculate the efficiency of this energy transfer.
A house is built with thick walls made of a material with a low thermal conductivity. Explain why the house cools down more slowly at night.
mastering.a: Low thermal conductivity means energy is transferred through the walls more slowly. Thicker walls also slow the rate of transfer. So energy is lost from the thermal store of the house to the surroundings more slowly, and the temperature falls more slowly.

mastering.q: The UK now generates more electricity from renewable resources, but still burns some fossil fuels. Explain why both are used.
mastering.a: Renewables (wind, solar) release no carbon dioxide while running and will not run out, so they reduce global warming. But wind and solar are not reliable: they depend on the weather and time of day. Fossil fuel power stations are reliable and can be switched on quickly to meet demand. So fossil fuels are still used to fill the gaps when demand is high or renewables produce too little.
indicativeContent: Renewables release no carbon dioxide while generating electricity
so they add less to global warming / climate change
Renewables will not run out; fossil fuels will
Wind and solar depend on the weather and time of day, so they are unreliable
Fossil fuel power stations are reliable and can be started quickly
so fossil fuels meet high demand or fill gaps when renewables produce too little
